$comment: The self-probe gate's cost ceiling, in seconds, checked in CI against the evidence the probe already writes. Raising this is a reviewable diff with a reason, which is the entire point: the gate went from 9.6 to 23.6 minutes across one merged pull request and nothing said a word. Growth is allowed; going unnoticed is not. Budget the TOTAL and never a per-fault average — the regression that prompted this raised the fault count from 59 to 91 while per-fault cost barely moved, so an average would have reported everything fine. Since #284 (PR #275) the ceiling is on the self-probe's NORMALIZED ELAPSED time at one fault-worker count (`unit`, `faultWorkers`): summed defender seconds rise when faults run side by side while the job gets faster, so the sum is printed and never gated.

measured.how: probe . --include-dirty --budget 180000 --cost, from scratch, idle developer machine, after the shared-defender cut
measured.note: LOCAL. Not comparable with measuredInCI and not what this budget is set from. The previous local from-scratch figure (1168 s, 129 faults) was taken on a contended machine, so 1168 -> 816 overstates the cut.

headroom: Ceilings are in normalized seconds (see `reference`). Headroom rule: the median of at least three from-scratch CI runs, normalized, plus the observed spread several times over; the first derivation (history, 2026-11-11, #255) used 9% over a 1.4% spread. The raw-seconds notes in earlier history entries describe the runner variance this replaced.

history.why: First budget. Set from the 804 s measurement after #73 cut the gate from 1414 s.

#82 added eight unit-defended faults (~30 s in CI) and main went 906 -> 981 s from scratch, red against 950. Re-pointing the two replay-defended calibration claims onto pure tests took it to 962 s. The remaining overage was the budget itself: set 18% over a local 804 s, it was 4.6% over the 906 s CI already measured. Raised to 1100 against the CI figure. The heavy claims it names — TG-ADMIT-NEEDS-ALL-KILLED 87 s, TG-PROBE-NEVER-EDITS-THE-TREE-IT-MEASURES 70 s, the two TG-MCP-* at 42 s — are the next #73-style cut, tracked separately.

The 0.8.1 field-report fixes added 6 claims and 14 faults (115 -> 129 faults, 690 -> 774 runs, +12.2%) and ci.yml measured 1123 s against 1100, over by 23 s. Two things make 1123 the wrong number to budget against, in opposite directions. It is LOW: the run restored a cache under the `self-evidence-` fallback key, so claims whose target and defenders were untouched reused their verdict, and this budget is defined against a from-scratch probe because the release job is from scratch. It is also not the whole story: 46 s of the growth was avoidable and already removed — the new calibration claim's tests are pure but were added to replay.test.mjs, whose scripted-corpus setup costs tens of seconds a run, and re-pointing them at calibration.test.mjs took that claim from 51 s to 4.9 s. A from-scratch local run of the same commit measured 1168 s on a contended machine. 1350 is ~14% over an expected from-scratch CI figure of ~1185, which is the same headroom rule that set 1100 against 962. Expected to come DOWN: the shared-defender cut below is the next piece of work and should return the gate to under 900 s.

Tightened from 1350 once a FROM-SCRATCH figure existed. 1350 was set defensively against a reuse-affected 1123 s, because this budget is defined against a from-scratch probe and none had run yet. release.yml then measured 1081 s at 129 faults / 774 runs on the v0.9.0 release commit with no reuse: 129 faults cost 1081 s against 115 faults at 999 s, so +82 s for +14 faults. 1230 is ~14% over 1081, the same headroom rule that set 1100 against 962. Leaving 1350 in place would have let a 25% regression pass unnoticed, which is the opposite of what this file is for.

The v0.10.1 release job supplied the next from-scratch measurement: 1210 s at 154 faults / 924 runs on 70e9d61. The old 1230 s ceiling therefore had only 1.7% headroom before this PR. The live-Homebrew-tap field fix adds one integration-defended claim, four faults and 24 runs; the Node 22 PR leg measured that claim at 53 s and the total at 1243 s with verdict reuse. Adding the deliberate 53 s to the cold release baseline projects ~1263 s. 1440 restores the established ~14% CI headroom without changing the 100 s per-claim ceiling.

PR #164 adds six claims and 15 faults (180 -> 195 in the claims file; the CI leg probed 186 of the 180+ with reuse) for the arid-measurement fixes and the claimspec signal bump. The Node 22 PR leg measured them at 85 s together, worst claim 22 s (TG-PROBE-CARRIES-THE-PERSISTENCE-SIGNAL, an end-to-end probe of a temporary repository, one fault) - all under the 100 s per-claim ceiling and of the shape nextCut.rule asks for (pure faults, unit defenders; the one e2e claim carries one fault on purpose). The leg went 1367 s on main to 1457 s, over 1440 by 17 s. Two figures matter and they disagree: the v0.13.0 release job measured 1113 s FROM SCRATCH at 180 faults / 1080 runs (run 35716135286, 53dd25d), while the PR leg measures the same worst claim at 91 s against 72 s cold - the PR runner is 25-30% slower, so the PR leg, not the release job, is what this ceiling actually binds. 1650 is ~13% over the 1457 s PR-leg figure, the same headroom rule as before; against the cold figure it is loose (~40%), which is why the per-claim ceiling stays at 100 s and why the next from-scratch release figure should be used to tighten this again, as 1350 -> 1230 was.

PR #174 run 36604096944 produced complete evidence with 220/220 faults killed and measured 1974 s against 1650. This is the post-optimization figure: the immediately preceding run cost 2205 s, and precise write-boundary defenders plus fault-specific dirty-preflight files removed 231 s before any ceiling change. Relative to the 1457 s / 186-fault PR leg that set 1650, the release candidate adds 34 faults and several intentionally integration-defended process/discovery contracts. The most expensive claims were 100, 82, 64, 61, and 52 s; none breached the separate 100 s per-claim gate. 2250 restores 14.0% headroom over the measured CI leg while keeping per-claim pressure intact.

PR #210 (the docs-audit fixes) adds 22 claims and 43 faults guarding a GitHub Action shell injection, verdict reuse surviving a changed --runner-cmd or a different runner, defender load failures never being reused, the pip wrapper's pinned fallback, init's all-or-nothing preflight, and runner-source binding. Run 38087039461 (ci.yml test (22)) measured 2438 s against 2250 with every fault killed; the new claims cost 365 s of it. Before raising anything the four init/helper claims were moved off test/init.test.mjs (43 tests, about 1.8 s a run) onto four single-purpose files and per-fault GitHub/GitLab helper files, re-probed 17/17 killed, which cuts an estimated 60-70 s. The rest is the deliberate coverage. 2700 is 10.7% above the pre-cut 2438 s leg and about 14% above the expected post-cut figure, the same CI-variance rule as 2250; the 100 s per-claim ceiling is unchanged and no new claim is near it (worst 43 s before the cut). Record the next leg's measured figure here and tighten if the cut landed bigger.

PR #245 (#237, --fault-workers) run 42934145571 measured 3077 s on the Node 22 leg with every fault killed (478/478), against 2700; PR #241 on the same base measured 2521 s at 444 faults. The 34 new faults guard the fault fan-out, the worktree-allocation lock, scratch git isolation and cleanup on cancellation, several of which are only provable end to end (a SIGINT mid-fan-out, a command budget expiring mid-fan-out, two concurrent probes). Before raising, those integration defenders were shortened (lock hold 1.5 -> 0.7 s, contention hold 250 -> 180 ms, per-run budget 1200 -> 800 ms, command budget 5 -> 3.5 s), an estimated 100 s. 3400 is 10.5% above the measured leg and about 14% above the expected post-cut figure, the same CI-variance rule as 2700; the 100 s per-claim ceiling is unchanged (worst new claim 58 s). The CI self-probe stays serial; --fault-workers would cut its wall time but not this cost, which sums per-record durations.

PR #244 (#239, the write boundary) run on head d1d6802 measured 3839 s on the Node 22 leg (567 faults, all killed) against 3400, over by 439 s. The branch merges main after #242 (probe --changed, external claims), #245 (fan-out) and #247 (--typecheck), which together took the fault count from 478 to 538 before this PR; this PR adds 29 faults in nine claims, measured at about 150 s locally (144 s runner time, the worst claim 25 s, under the 100 s per-claim ceiling). The rest of the growth is not this PR's and is not decomposed here. 4300 is 12% above the measured leg, the same CI-variance rule as 3400.

The ceiling goes DOWN from 4300. PR #254 (the suite runtime budget) ran the self-probe at 592 faults, all killed, on two heads with identical claims and defenders: 2901 s (run 43062166737, Node 22 leg) and 3366 s (run 43064382390, same leg); the earlier CI measurement was 3396 s. 3366 + 14% = 3837, rounded to 3850. The 465 s spread between two runs of the same code is the CI variance this headroom exists for (the cause of the lower run was not isolated). No claim or defender changed in this PR; the 4300 set at 3839 s / 567 faults was a ceiling over a run that no longer reproduces.

3850 was set the same day from two samples (2901 s and 3366 s) and was wrong within hours: PR #230, a workflow-actions bump with identical claims and defenders, measured 4159 s on the Node 22 leg (run for head 6ddb8ac) and failed by 309 s. Four CI measurements of the same 592 faults now span 2876 s to 4159 s, a 45% spread that is the runner, not the suite. 4159 + 14% = 4741, rounded to 4750. A ceiling in summed seconds cannot be tight while runner speed varies this much; normalizing the cost by a per-run speed reference is the real fix and is tracked as an issue.

The ceiling is now in NORMALIZED seconds (#255), so it is not comparable with the raw ceilings above it. Four from-scratch CI runs of the same 604 faults (verdict reuse off, 0 reused records) measured 2730, 3334, 3913 and 3963 s raw, a 45% spread, on runners whose reference workload took 166, 202, 237 and 238 ms. Normalized by the factor against baselineMs 200 they are 3278, 3300, 3306 and 3323 s, a 1.4% spread; median 3303 s (runs in `reference.runs`). 3600 is the median plus 9%: about six times the observed spread, kept because four runs on three machine speeds do not bound a fourth runner class. It replaces 4750 raw, which sat 19% above the slowest raw measurement and 74% above the fastest. Per-claim ceiling unchanged, now also normalized.

PR #262 (fixes from the independent and white-box verification of 0.22.1) adds 28 faults in 12 claims, from 604 to 632, and ci.yml test (22) measured 3946 normalized seconds (4828 raw, reference 241/249 ms, factor 1.22, 0 reused records) against 3600, over by 346. The median of the four runs that set 3600 was 3303 at 604 faults, 5.5 s a fault; the new claims run 7-12 s a fault because their honest defenders are end-to-end: real probes of a throwaway repository (scope state, a lone timing-out fault, the progress stream after a budget expiry, a written partial document), a real child process for the signal exits, and the Python engine on two fixture claims. Before raising, the two heaviest were cut (the budget-expiry defenders probe two or three claims, not four), an estimated 80 s. 4200 is 9% above the expected post-cut figure of about 3860, the same rule that set 3600; the 100 s per-claim ceiling is unchanged and every new claim is under it (worst 74 s locally before the cut).

PR #275 (#270, fast by default) makes the CI self-probe fan out (--fault-workers auto: 2 at a time on the 4-CPU runner, every kill confirmed by a run alone) and adds 34 faults in 9 claims (632 to 666). Two from-scratch measurements of ci.yml test (22), 0 reused records, every fault killed: 4243 normalized s (3812 raw, factor 0.90) and, after the cuts below, 4215 (4286 raw, factor 1.02), against 4200. GROWTH: the new claims cost about 190 s raw; before this raise 601 s raw of CLI-acceptance defenders were moved onto unit tests (45 s) and a 38 s helper fault became an ignore entry. INFLATION FROM OVERLAP: with two faults running at once each run takes longer, so the summed per-run seconds this ceiling counts rise while the job gets faster: the same runs took 1626 s and 1839 s wall-clock (1807 and 1803 normalized) against 4243 and 4215 summed. raccioly/testguard#284 moves the gate to normalized elapsed time; check-cost-budget.mjs now prints normalized elapsed and the fault-worker width beside the summed figure to give it a baseline. 4650 is 9% above the higher measurement, the rule that set 3600 and 4200; the per-claim ceiling is unchanged.

The series resets: the unit changed from summed defender seconds to normalized ELAPSED seconds at 2 fault workers (#284, PR #275). PR #275 makes the CI self-probe fan out by default (2 at a time on the 4-CPU runner, every kill confirmed by a run alone), and from then on summed seconds rose while the job got faster: from-scratch runs on its heads summed 4243, 4215 and 4812 normalized seconds while their elapsed time was 1807, 1803 and 2041 normalized seconds. Growth since the last entry: 666 to 723 faults; claims new on main since the branch started cost 232 s summed and this PR's 302 s; elapsed per fault 2.71, 2.71 and 2.82 normalized seconds. The ceiling comes from the one from-scratch run on the final code (2041 s normalized elapsed, head a5039ec, 723/723 killed, 1823 s wall-clock, factor 0.89) plus 12% because fewer than three runs exist on it: 2286, rounded to 2290. Tighten it from main's next three from-scratch runs by the headroom rule. A run at another fault-worker count fails closed (fault-workers-mismatch), like the runner-class check.

Two from-scratch runs on the final code of PR #275 now exist: 2041 normalized elapsed seconds (head a5039ec, 723 faults, factor 0.89) and 2000 (head f94bea0, 726 faults, factor 1.01; summed 4675, not gated), every fault killed. Median 2020.5 plus 12% (the two-sample rule this series started with) is 2263, rounded to 2270. Tighten it from main's next three from-scratch runs by the file's headroom rule.

A NEW CONFIGURATION, not a raise of the unsharded ceiling (2270, unchanged, still what an unsharded probe is judged by): the full self-probe is now 4 shards by defender set, so its ceilings are keyed by the shard count as well as faultWorkers and the sum counts per-shard startup. From-scratch sharded run on the final slicing (PR #299, run 43257268049, 780 faults, every fault killed): sum 2121 normalized s, shard walls 535 / 540 / 540 / 506 (slowest 540). The unsharded runs this configuration replaces measured 2000-2041 normalized s, so sharding costs about 4% in total compute; the growth in this PR is 54 new faults (726 -> 780), about 4.6% of recorded cost (about 97 s of the sum). Slicing by claim id instead measured 2255 s (573 s slowest), which is why the slices follow defender sets. Ceilings are that run plus the two-sample 12% (2121 x 1.12 = 2376 -> 2380; 540 x 1.12 = 605 -> 610) because only one run of the final slicing existed when this was written; a second run on this commit follows and this entry is updated to the median of both. Tighten from main's next three from-scratch sharded runs by the file's headroom rule.

measuredInCI.how: release.yml test: probe . --budget 180000 --cost, from scratch on the v0.13.0 release commit. No verdict reuse, which is what this budget is defined against.

prLeg.note: ci.yml test (22) on PR #210 before the init/helper defender split; every fault killed. New claims cost 365 s of it.

before.note: ci.yml test (22) on PR #174 after the targeted defender-cost cuts; complete evidence was 220/220 killed. The run may include restored evidence costs, but this is the leg the ceiling gates and the separate 100 s per-claim ceiling remains unchanged.
the v0.10.1 release job; 1113 s at 180 faults means the v0.11-0.13 claims were cheap and the release runner got faster, not that the gate shrank

reuseAffected.note: ci.yml figures are NOT comparable with this one. Its cache restore-key chain ends in a bare 'self-evidence-' prefix, so any previous evidence can be restored regardless of claims hash, and a reused record contributes what it cost when it was last probed on another runner. The same commit reported 1123 s and then 1025 s. Correctness is unaffected - TG-REUSE-NEVER-CROSSES-A-FAULT-EDIT re-probes any changed fault - only the reported total moves.

done.why: faults classify(), a pure function; was defended by negative-control.test.mjs, which spawns real runners against fixture repositories
faults labelDiff(), pure; was defended by replay.test.mjs, which builds a scripted git corpus

nextCut.expectedInCI: The projected ~145 s cut was real, but later behavior coverage spent the savings: v0.10.1 measured 1210 s from scratch at 154 faults. Future cuts must be confirmed against a release job and must not trade end-to-end coverage for seconds.
nextCut.remaining: The eight claims still on negative-control.test.mjs and replay.test.mjs fault probe.mjs, the runners and git-walking code, where the expensive fixture is the point. Forcing those onto unit tests would trade real end-to-end coverage for seconds.
nextCut.rule: A claim whose fault lands in a pure module should have a pure defender. All three cuts above fit that shape, and so did the 51 s calibration claim before them. This is mechanically checkable — compare the imports of the faulted file against those of its defenders — and is the shape of a future `claims --lint`.

perClaim.why: A SECOND ceiling, because neither unit works alone. The total can only ever be raised - claims should grow forever - so a number that always goes up stops being read. A per-fault average is worse: the regression that prompted this budget raised the fault count 59 to 91 while per-fault cost barely moved, so an average would have reported everything fine. The measured pathology is per-CLAIM, and specifically a claim naming an expensive SHARED defender file, because a claim pays for every test in the file it names. TG-ADMIT-NEEDS-ALL-KILLED costs 67 s for ONE fault; a new calibration claim landed at 51 s for two purely by being written into replay.test.mjs rather than calibration.test.mjs, and re-pointing it took it to 4.9 s. The total absorbed that silently; this does not. Since #284 the per-claim figure is still SUMMED seconds, and under the default fan-out those are inflated by overlap (a run takes longer while another fault is in flight); it stays a gate for now, and #284 tracks deciding its unit.
perClaim.rule: No new claim may be worse than the worst we already have. 75 s sits just above today's worst, so the ceiling stays meaningful as claims are added and should be tightened as the shared-defender cut lands.

todayWorst.where: CI (ci.yml test 22); the same claim measures 66.5 s locally

perClaim.calibratedAgainst: CI, never local. 75 s was set from a local 66.5 s and tripped on the very first CI run, where the same claim costs 87 s — a CI runner is materially slower, and this file already says so for the total: 950 s was 18% over local 804 s but only 4.6% over CI's 906 s, and the first PR adding any claim tripped it. The same error, one level down. 100 s is ~15% over the CI worst.

reference.how: Normalization unit, not a hardware claim: the speed factor is (mean of the before/after reference medians) / baselineMs, and normalized seconds are raw seconds / factor. When the two medians differ by more than maxDrift the factor is the FASTER median over baselineMs instead (the pessimistic reading), so a runner that slowed down mid-run cannot hide growth. `cpus` and `platform` are the runner class the baseline was taken on (the Node 22 leg's 4-CPU Linux runners): the reference tracks probe speed within one class of machine and not across classes (an 18-core laptop read 177 ms, inside the CI range, and runs the probe far faster than CI), so a measurement from another CPU count or platform fails the check with `reference-runner-mismatch` and is never normalized. Taking a baseline on another class means a new baselineMs, cpus, platform and ceiling together. 200 ms was fixed before any CI measurement, near the median of the four from-scratch CI runs in `history` (166-238 ms on the Node 22 leg's 4-CPU runners). Changing it rescales every ceiling in this file; changing the workload in .github/scripts/measure-reference.mjs requires re-taking it in the same pull request.

sharded.how: The full self-probe split into 4 shards by defender set (shard-probe.mjs), each on its own 4-CPU runner at faultWorkers 2, each normalized by the reference it timed itself. `seconds` bounds the SUM of the shards (total compute); `slowestShardSeconds` bounds the slowest shard (what a person waits for). The configuration is part of the ceiling's validity, like faultWorkers: a run with another number of shards fails closed. Derived 2026-11-12 (#294), see the last history entry.
